articles.title: Nine Games, Zero Wins — Then They Beat the World Champions. India's Hockey Team Just Ended Its Misery in Rotterdam.
articles.excerpt: Two days after their worst Pro League campaign hit rock bottom, India dismantled reigning world champions Germany 3-1 — on the same night Manpreet Singh became the most-capped player in Indian hockey history.
articles.image_caption: Manpreet Singh, who became the most-capped player in Indian hockey history during India's 3-1 win over Germany
articles.nri_angle: Hockey is India's most decorated Olympic sport — eight golds and the deepest national sporting memory — and this win over the reigning world champions, on the night captain-class veteran Manpreet Singh became India's most-capped player ever, is the kind of redemption story that resonates with NRIs who inherited that history from grandparents who watched India dominate the game.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: America's Cricket Season Opened With Its Highest-Ever Chase. A 41-Year-Old From Pretoria Made 113 to Win It.
articles.excerpt: Faf du Plessis, captain of the Chennai-owned Texas Super Kings, hauled down a mountainous 221 in 18.3 overs to launch Major League Cricket's fourth season in Grand Prairie — the Dallas suburb that has become the capital of cricket in America.
articles.image_caption: Faf du Plessis, captain of the Texas Super Kings, whose unbeaten 113 sealed a record chase on the opening night of Major League Cricket 2026
articles.nri_angle: Major League Cricket is the most tangible expression of cricket's American chapter — a professional league built in the US suburbs the Indian and South Asian diaspora calls home, with Grand Prairie near Dallas as its capital. The Texas Super Kings are co-owned by the IPL's Chennai Super Kings, and the record opening-night chase gives NRIs in the US a top-tier league in their own time zone, their own city, and a professional pathway for the next generation that did not exist a decade ago.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Injury He Hid, the Coach He Left: Neeraj Chopra Returns to the Runway in Doha
articles.excerpt: After nine months away — his longest absence since Olympic gold — India's greatest track-and-field star opens his 2026 season on Friday with a startling admission about Tokyo, and a quiet rebellion against the foreign-expert model: he has gone back to an Indian coach.
articles.image_caption: Neeraj Chopra, India's double Olympic medallist, returns to competition at the Doha Diamond League after a nine-month injury layoff
articles.nri_angle: Neeraj Chopra is the Indian diaspora's rarest icon — an individual-sport world conqueror with no cricketing safety net — and NRIs across the US, UK and Canada set alarms to watch him compete. His return at the Doha Diamond League after a nine-month injury layoff carries an extra charge: he has left the legendary Czech coach Jan Zelezny to train under an Indian mentor, Jaiveer 'Jay' Chaudhary, a quiet rejection of the foreign-expert premium the diaspora knows so well, and a bet on his own instincts ahead of the Commonwealth and Asian Games.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: She Is 18, She Beat the World No. 10 in Washington, and She Is India's Best Shot at an Olympic Squash Medal
articles.excerpt: Anahat Singh has cracked the world's top 20, defended her Indian Open title in Mumbai and become the youngest Asian woman ever to climb that high. With squash entering the Olympics for the first time at LA 2028, the teenager from Delhi is carrying a sport — and a diaspora — on her shoulders.
articles.image_caption: Indian squash great Joshna Chinappa, pictured after a junior title win — part of the generation that paved the way for teenage No. 1 Anahat Singh
articles.nri_angle: Squash is quietly one of the diaspora's sports — South Asian families fill racquet clubs in New Jersey, suburban London and the Greater Toronto Area — yet the community rarely sees itself represented at the elite level. Anahat Singh, 18, of Delhi, has cracked the world's top 20 (the youngest Asian woman ever to do so), beaten the world No. 10, and become India's best hope for a medal when squash debuts at the LA 2028 Olympics. A composed, fearless role model for NRI families and their daughters.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: She Is 21, She Is From Hyderabad, and She Just Broke a World Record on the Germans' Home Range
articles.excerpt: At the ISSF World Cup in Munich, Esha Singh shot 43 out of 50 to win the women's 25m pistol gold — a score that now stands as both the senior and junior world record. She beat the reigning Olympic champion and a former world champion to do it. India's quiet shooting empire just got a new face.
articles.image_caption: Indian pistol shooter Esha Singh, who set senior and junior 25m pistol world records (43/50) to win gold at the 2026 ISSF World Cup in Munich
articles.nri_angle: Shooting rarely makes the diaspora highlight reels that cricket and chess command, yet it has quietly become one of India's most reliable medal factories — a discipline where Indian women routinely beat established European and East Asian powers on their home ranges. Esha Singh, 21, from Hyderabad, outshot the reigning Olympic champion and a former world champion in Munich to set senior and junior world records, a quieter, more precise kind of pride for NRIs to follow.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: She Coached at MIT, Then the Grizzlies. Now Sonia Raman Is the First Indian-Origin Head Coach in the WNBA — and the Hardest Part Has Only Just Begun.
articles.excerpt: A walk-on guard who became a lawyer, then the winningest coach in MIT history, then the first Indian-American woman on an NBA bench, Raman took over the Seattle Storm this season. At 3-12, the rebuild is brutal — but the barrier she broke is permanent.
articles.image_caption: Seattle Storm guard Flau'jae Johnson during the 2026 WNBA season, Sonia Raman's first as head coach
articles.nri_angle: Sonia Raman is the first person of Indian origin to be a head coach in the WNBA — and earlier was the first Indian-American woman to coach in the NBA — a barrier-breaking career that offers South Asian families in America a powerful counter-example to the idea that professional sport is not a serious path.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Son of Kerala Is About to Make World Cup History — in Qatar's Colours
articles.excerpt: Tahsin Mohammed Jamshid, the Doha-born winger with roots in Kannur, stands on the brink of becoming the first footballer of Indian origin to play at a FIFA World Cup.
articles.image_caption: The Qatar national football team, which 20-year-old Kerala-origin winger Tahsin Jamshid represents at the 2026 World Cup
articles.nri_angle: For decades, football-obsessed Kerala has poured its passion into supporting Brazil, Argentina and Germany at the World Cup without ever having a player of its own on the stage. Tahsin Jamshid — born in Doha to Malayali parents from Kannur — is poised to become the first footballer of Indian origin to play at a FIFA World Cup, a landmark for the Gulf's vast Malayali expatriate community and a bittersweet milestone for an India whose own men's team has never qualified.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: America's Cricket League Begins Its Fourth Season Tonight. It Was Built in the Suburbs the Diaspora Calls Home.
articles.excerpt: Major League Cricket returns June 18 with Steve Smith, Glenn Maxwell and Faf du Plessis on the marquee — but the league's real project is the American-raised, largely Indian-origin core now sharing a dressing room with them. From Grand Prairie to a sold-out Oakland Coliseum final, this is the diaspora's home team.
articles.image_caption: Grand Prairie Stadium in Texas, a purpose-built home of Major League Cricket
articles.nri_angle: Major League Cricket is the diaspora's own professional league — funded largely by Indian-American capital, staged in the U.S. suburbs with the densest South Asian populations, and increasingly powered by American-raised, mostly Indian-origin players like Monank Patel and Saurabh Netravalkar, turning a game of cultural preservation into a credible profession for immigrant kids.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: He Beat Carlsen Twice and the World Champion Once. In Oslo, a 20-Year-Old From Chennai Showed Why India Now Runs Chess.
articles.excerpt: R Praggnanandhaa's Norway Chess title is the latest sign of a generational shift: a country that had one world champion in 2013 now has the reigning world champion, the tournament's winner, and a clutch of 2700-rated players barely out of their teens. For a global game increasingly played in Indian living rooms, the future has an accent.
articles.image_caption: R Praggnanandhaa, who won Norway Chess 2026 ahead of Magnus Carlsen and world champion Gukesh Dommaraju
articles.nri_angle: India's chess surge runs straight through diaspora living rooms — the same low-cost, high-prestige game that Indian-American and Indian-British families have embraced en masse is now producing the world's most exciting young grandmasters, making players like Praggnanandhaa and Gukesh proof of concept for a particular immigrant bet.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Two Indian Teenagers Are One Win From a Wimbledon Junior Main Draw. A Decade Ago, This Was Unthinkable.
articles.excerpt: Maaya Rajeshwaran Revathi, seeded No. 1 in girls' qualifying, and 17-year-old Hitesh Chauhan both reached the final qualifying round at Roehampton — backed by academy training and corporate money that earlier generations never had.
articles.image_caption: The National Tennis Centre at Roehampton, the venue where Wimbledon junior qualifying is played

Khelnow — Maaya Rajeshwaran wins US Open 2025 opening match; Hitesh Chauhan bows out
ITF Tennis — Maaya Rajeshwaran Revathi player profile

articles.nri_angle: The junior tennis pipeline India's rising players climb runs through the US college and ITF circuits where much of the diaspora lives, making these teenagers' breakthroughs personal and aspirational for Indian-American families.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: From a Bakersfield Muni to Shinnecock: The Gujarati-American Who Skipped Med School and Became the First IGPL Golfer at a Major
articles.excerpt: Manav Shah was supposed to be a doctor. Instead, the California-born son of Gujarati immigrants ground his way through Latin American mini-tours, rebuilt his game on an Indian circuit during a chance detour, and survived golf's toughest qualifier to reach the U.S. Open.
articles.image_caption: The first tee at Shinnecock Hills during the U.S. Open, where Manav Shah makes his Major debut
articles.nri_angle: Manav Shah is the immigrant-family story in miniature — a California-born son of Gujarati parents who chose golf over the expected path into medicine, kept his heritage alive through an Indian league, and now becomes the first IGPL golfer at a Major, a marker of how deep diaspora golf has grown.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Four Days After a Super Over Meltdown, India A Answered With 319 and a 101-Run Rout to Reach the Final
articles.excerpt: Three fifties — Tilak Varma's 59, plus 58 each from Priyansh Arya and Kumar Kushagra — and Nishant Sindhu's 4/31 carried India A into the tri-series final in Dambulla. It is the same A-team shop window that has been quietly minting India's senior internationals.
articles.image_caption: India A captain Tilak Varma, who top-scored with 59 as India A reached the tri-series final in Dambulla
articles.nri_angle: NRIs follow India's senior XI obsessively, but the A-team in Dambulla is where the next Gill or Jaiswal is being forged — the names on this team sheet are the players the diaspora will be watching for India over the next decade.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Same Week the Men Finished Last, India's Women Are Unbeaten in Auckland — and One Step From a Pro League Promotion
articles.excerpt: India's women's hockey team beat the USA 3-2 from two goals down, then edged Japan 2-1 to reach the FIH Nations Cup semi-finals with a game to spare. Win the tournament in New Zealand and they are promoted to the 2026-27 FIH Pro League — the elite circuit the men's side just endured a winless season in.
articles.image_caption: India captain Salima Tete, who scored against Japan as India reached the FIH Women's Nations Cup semi-finals in Auckland
articles.nri_angle: Hockey carries deep heritage for Indians abroad, and a Nations Cup win would promote India's women — led by athletes from Jharkhand's Simdega belt and the northeast — to the elite FIH Pro League, putting them on the same broadcast calendars the diaspora already follows for cricket and football.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Women Just Posted Their Highest-Ever World Cup Total. Mandhana and Shafali Took 11 Overs to Bury the Netherlands.
articles.excerpt: Smriti Mandhana (74 off 47) and Shafali Verma (55 off 38) shared a 115-run opening stand and brought up India's joint-fastest team fifty in Women's T20 World Cup history. India's 209 for 5 at Headingley was the most they have ever made at a World Cup — and a debutant Netherlands side never stood a chance.
articles.image_caption: Smriti Mandhana, who top-scored with 74 off 47 balls as India posted their highest-ever Women's T20 World Cup total
articles.nri_angle: India's women have never won a senior global title, and a generation of NRI families in Britain has watched them grow into genuine contenders — Headingley, in the heart of Yorkshire's South Asian community, drew a vocal, flag-waving diaspora crowd.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Two Centuries, a 224-Run Stand, and India's 500th ODI Win: Gill and Kishan Sink Afghanistan in Lucknow
articles.excerpt: Shubman Gill's ninth ODI hundred and Ishan Kishan's maiden century carried India to a 15-run victory at Lucknow, sealing the three-match series 2-0 with a game to spare — and handing the country a landmark 500th win in one-day internationals.
articles.image_caption: Shubman Gill scored his ninth ODI century to lead India past Afghanistan in the second ODI at Lucknow
articles.nri_angle: India's white-ball rebuild under captain Shubman Gill is appointment viewing for the cricket-following Indian diaspora, and a milestone 500th ODI win, twin centuries, and a touch of old-fashioned sportsmanship make for exactly the kind of storyline NRIs forward to family group chats within minutes.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: 274 Days Without a Throw. On Friday, Neeraj Chopra Finally Returns — in the City Where He First Broke 90 Metres.
articles.excerpt: India's two-time Olympic javelin medallist will open his 2026 season at the Doha Diamond League on June 19, his first competition since a back injury wrecked his World Championships last September. He walks into a nine-man field led by a Sri Lankan who has already thrown 92.62m this year.
articles.image_caption: Neeraj Chopra, India's two-time Olympic javelin medallist, returns at the Doha Diamond League on June 19
articles.nri_angle: Neeraj Chopra is India's most globally followed track-and-field athlete — the man who ended a 100-year wait for Olympic athletics gold — and NRIs across the US, UK, Canada and the Gulf treat his competitions as appointment viewing, often setting alarms for awkward hours to watch a single throw.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Nine Games, Zero Wins: India's Hockey Team Is Having Its Worst Pro League Ever — at the Worst Possible Time
articles.excerpt: India sit eighth of nine in the FIH Pro League with four points and a minus-17 goal difference, having not won a single match in regulation. With the World Cup and Asian Games months away, Craig Fulton's side faces Germany in Rotterdam needing to prove the slump is a blip, not a warning.
articles.image_caption: India captain Harmanpreet Singh receiving the Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award; his side is enduring a winless 2025-26 FIH Pro League campaign
articles.nri_angle: Hockey is India's national sport by heritage, and NRIs across the US, UK, Canada and Australia follow the Pro League on Star Sports and JioHotstar. A winless campaign just as India should be peaking for the World Cup and Asian Games lands hard with a diaspora that treats the team's revival as a point of pride.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A 21-Year-Old From Madurai Just Won an NCAA Title in Eugene. It Was India's First in Four Years.
articles.excerpt: Selva Prabhu leapt 16.92m at Hayward Field to take the 2026 NCAA Outdoor triple jump crown for Kansas State — India's first NCAA outdoor athletics title since Tejaswin Shankar in 2022, and the latest proof that the American college system has become a real pathway for Indian track and field.
articles.image_caption: Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon, where Selva Prabhu won the 2026 NCAA Outdoor triple jump title for Kansas State
articles.nri_angle: Selva Prabhu's NCAA title shows how the American college system has become a real development pathway for Indian track-and-field talent — a pipeline diaspora families already know intimately, now producing national champions.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Month After the First Indian-Heritage Major Champion, the U.S. Open Has Its Deepest-Ever Diaspora Field
articles.excerpt: Aaron Rai arrives at Shinnecock Hills as a major winner, Akshay Bhatia as a ranked contender, and two qualifiers complete the largest contingent of golfers of Indian origin the championship has ever seen.
articles.image_caption: Akshay Bhatia at a PGA Tour event
articles.nri_angle: For the first time, golfers of Indian origin are competing at a U.S. Open not as curiosities but as major champions, ranked contenders and hard-earned qualifiers — a milestone moment for South Asian families across the US, UK and India who have embraced the sport.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: She Outranked Kohli and Rohit on a List Headlined by LeBron. Smriti Mandhana Is the Only Indian on TIME's 100 Most Influential in Sports.
articles.excerpt: The India vice-captain is the lone Indian athlete — and one of just two cricketers — on TIME's 2026 list, placed in the 'Titans' tier alongside Messi, Ronaldo and Alcaraz.
articles.image_caption: India women's cricket vice-captain Smriti Mandhana, the only Indian on TIME's 2026 list of the 100 Most Influential People in Sports

The Hindu BusinessLine — Smriti Mandhana only Indian among TIME magazine's 100 most influential sportspersons

articles.nri_angle: Seeing an Indian woman cricketer ranked among the most influential figures in world sport — ahead of the men's-game superstars the diaspora grew up idolizing — reframes what representation looks like for the next generation growing up abroad.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: An Auckland Sikh in the No. 10 Shirt Played the Full 90. No Footballer of Indian Origin Had Ever Started a World Cup Match Before.
articles.excerpt: Sarpreet Singh, born in Auckland to a Jalandhar family, started New Zealand's 2-2 draw with Iran in Los Angeles — a milestone no Indian-heritage player had reached in 96 years of the tournament. Vikash Dhorasoo, the only one before him, had only ever come off the bench.
articles.image_caption: Sarpreet Singh training with Bayern Munich in 2019; he became the first Indian-origin player to start a World Cup match
articles.nri_angle: Sarpreet Singh, born in Auckland to a Jalandhar Punjabi family, became the first footballer of Indian origin ever to start a World Cup match — a surrogate source of pride for a diaspora whose own national team has never qualified.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: He Beat the World No. 9 on Clay in Paris. Now the Indian-American Faces the One Surface He Has Never Played as a Pro.
articles.excerpt: Nishesh Basavareddy, the 21-year-old from Carmel, Indiana, whose parents emigrated from Nellore, has been seeded No. 26 for Wimbledon qualifying starting June 22. His career grass-court record on tour: zero matches.
articles.image_caption: Nishesh Basavareddy, the Indian-American seeded No. 26 in Wimbledon qualifying, in action in 2024
articles.nri_angle: Basavareddy is a Telugu-heritage, Nellore-rooted Indian-American chasing a Wimbledon main-draw debut — the closest the subcontinent's diaspora has to a homegrown singles contender at a Grand Slam, even as the talent was developed entirely in the United States.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Two North American Teams, One Ontario Ground, and a Squad List That Reads Like a Punjab Phone Book.
articles.excerpt: Canada close out a six-match ODI tri-series against the Netherlands and the USA on Tuesday in King City. The cricket is about 2027 World Cup points. The story is who is playing it — sides built almost entirely of South Asian migrants.
articles.image_caption: Saad Bin Zafar, captain of Canada, who led the side in the 2026 tri-nation ODI series in King City, Ontario
articles.nri_angle: Two North American national cricket teams — Canada and the USA — are built almost entirely of Indian, Pakistani and South Asian migrants, and this Ontario tri-series is where the diaspora's lost cricketing talent now competes for a 2027 World Cup berth.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
